caption: Mercury is element 80, a metal that is liquid at room temperature. The small drawing is methylmercury: mercury bonded to one carbon carrying three hydrogens (CH₃). Bacteria in lake mud make it, and it is the form that builds up in fish.

Lead is element 82, one of the heaviest stable elements. In tap water it almost always comes from pipes, solder and fixtures rather than the bedrock. It is also where the uranium–radium–radon chain ends: lead-206.

Arsenic is element 33, directly under phosphorus (outlined). Elements in the same column behave alike, which is how arsenate slips into the body's phosphate chemistry. In bedrock wells here it is natural, released from the rock.

Uranium in the bedrock decays, one step at a time, into lead. Radon (gold) is the only gas in the chain, so it can leave the rock for well water and basement air. Its half-life is 3.8 days: it decays in the air you breathe into short-lived radioactive metals. Each box shows the element's mass number and, under it, its half-life.

Uranium in the bedrock decays, one step at a time, into lead. Radium (gold) is one step, with a half-life of about 1,600 years. It sits in the same column as calcium and barium, so the body carries it where calcium goes, into bone. Each box shows the element's mass number and, under it, its half-life.

Iron is element 26; manganese (outlined) sits next door at 25. Neighbours behave alike: both dissolve when well water runs short of oxygen, and both drop out as specks when the water meets air (iron orange, manganese black).

Manganese is element 25, next door to iron (outlined). Both dissolve when well water runs short of oxygen, which is why they turn up together in the same wells. Out of the tap, manganese stains black and iron orange.

Barium is element 56, in the same column as calcium (outlined). Elements in a column behave alike, so dissolved barium is carried where calcium goes, including into bone. It weathers out of shale and limestone.

Sodium is element 11. With chlorine (outlined, element 17) it makes table salt, NaCl; in water the two separate into ions that travel on their own. Plateau wells are high in sodium partly because the shale trades its sodium for the water's calcium.

Chlorine is element 17. In water it is chloride (Cl⁻), the half of salt left after sodium (outlined) separates from it. Chloride does not react, stick to soil or break down, which makes it the tracer for road salt.

Every corner of the zigzag is a carbon, and every carbon is wrapped in fluorines (green): the carbon–fluorine bond is the strongest single bond in organic chemistry, which is why nothing in nature breaks it. The name reads the drawing: per-fluoro (every hydrogen swapped for fluorine), octane (8 carbons), sulfonate (the S with three O's, the head that dissolves in water).

The same fluorinated tail as PFOS, but a different head: a carboxylic acid (a C with two O's) instead of a sulfonate. Octanoic acid means an 8-carbon acid, counting the head's carbon. The green fluorines are the part nothing in nature can break.
PFOS with two carbons fewer: hexane means 6. Shortening the chain was the industry's answer to PFOS. Shorter chains leave the body faster but move through soil and past filters more easily.

Four small molecules, each one carbon holding one hydrogen and three halogens: chlorine (teal) or bromine (tan). Start from methane (CH₄) and swap three hydrogens. All chlorine makes chloroform, and each bromine swapped in makes the next one. The bromine comes from traces of bromide in the source water.

Top left is vinegar's acid (acetic acid). Swap one, two or three hydrogens on its first carbon for chlorine or bromine and you get the five regulated haloacetic acids. They form the way trihalomethanes do: chlorine meeting natural organic matter in the water.

A six-member ring of four carbons and two oxygens (red), facing each other at positions 1 and 4. The oxygens let it mix completely with water, so it travels with groundwater and slips past carbon filters.

One nitrogen (blue) holding three oxygens, with a negative charge overall. Nitrate is nitrogen at its most oxidised: where the nitrogen in manure, septic waste and fertiliser ends up once bacteria are done with it. It dissolves fully and does not stick to soil, so it rides with water to wells.

The hexagon with alternating double lines is benzene, the ring at the heart of oil chemistry. Toluene is benzene with one carbon stub (a methyl group) attached. Every unlabelled corner is a carbon with hidden hydrogens.

Benzene with two methyl stubs. Where the second stub sits gives three versions: ortho (neighbours), meta (one apart), para (opposite). Same atoms, different shape: these are called isomers. Total xylenes is the sum of all three.

A ring of seven amino acids made by cyanobacteria. The long side chain ending in a benzene hexagon is Adda, found only in microcystins and the closely related nodularin; it is the part that grips a liver enzyme. The closed ring is part of why boiling does not destroy it.

Phosphate: one phosphorus (orange) at the centre of four oxygens. Total phosphorus counts every form, dissolved or stuck to soil particles. It is the nutrient that limits algae in fresh water: add phosphate and a lake turns green.

Not a molecule but a cell: Escherichia coli, a rod about 2 micrometres long. Labs do not test for every germ; they count E. coli because it lives mainly in the guts of warm-blooded animals, so finding it means fecal matter reached the water, and whatever germs travel with it.

Left, an oxygen molecule: two oxygen atoms double-bonded, O₂. Right, a water molecule. Dissolved oxygen is O₂ slipped between water molecules, not the O inside H₂O. Cold water holds more; warm, still water and rotting algae use it up.
